findings.title: limitFunction drops all arguments passed to the limited wrapper
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is declared as `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it never captures or forwards the caller's arguments to `function_`.
findings.impact: Any wrapped function that depends on parameters receives `undefined` values. This breaks the TypeScript contract that the returned function has the same arguments and also breaks repository examples such as the benchmark call `limitedTask(delay, i)`.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 implements a zero-argument wrapper; index.d.ts:133-136 returns `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`; benchmark.js:192-194 calls the limited function with `(delay, i)`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused Node probe imported the current source in memory and ran `limitFunction(async (a, b) => [a, b], {concurrency: 1})('left', 'right')`; observed `limitFunction args: [null,null]` because JSON stringifies undefined array elements as null. The same probe against `HEAD:index.js` returned `["left","right"]`.

findings.title: limit.map passes undefined as the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper now special-cases `Array.isArray(iterable)` and passes `undefined` for the index when the iterable is a Set, generator, or array iterator.
findings.impact: The documented `limit.map` contract says every mapper receives the item and its index, so callers using Set or iterator inputs for indexing, batching, keys, or order-aware transforms silently get undefined instead of 0, 1, 2, ...
findings.evidence: readme.md:78-85 documents `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`; index.d.ts:30-43 types the mapper index as `number`; index.js:108-112 passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused Node probe ran `pLimit(2).map(new Set(['a','b','c']), (_value, index) => index)` and `pLimit(2).map(['x','y','z'].values(), (_value, index) => index)`; observed `undefined,undefined,undefined` for both. The same probe against `HEAD:index.js` returned `0,1,2` for both.

findings.title: Options-object default enables rejectOnClear despite the documented default false
findings.cause: The options destructuring changed to `rejectOnClear = true`, so `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` opts into rejecting queued promises even when the caller did not request it.
findings.impact: Code following the documented default can start receiving AbortError rejections from `clearQueue()` after switching from numeric concurrency to the equivalent options object, potentially failing `Promise.all` flows and creating unexpected rejection handling requirements.
findings.evidence: readme.md:46-52 and readme.md:149-155 state `rejectOnClear` is boolean with default false; index.d.ts:99-106 also states default false; index.js:6-8 defaults the option to true.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused Node probe created `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1})`, queued one running and one pending task, called `clearQueue()`, and raced the pending promise against a timeout. Observed `default object clearQueue pending status: rejected:AbortError`. The same probe against `HEAD:index.js` observed `still-pending`.

findings.title: rejectOnClear runtime validation accepts falsey non-booleans
findings.cause: The type guard is gated by the option's truthiness: `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`. Falsey non-booleans such as 0, empty string, or null bypass validation.
findings.impact: JavaScript consumers can pass invalid option values without the TypeError promised by the runtime validation, creating behavior that diverges from the public `boolean` option contract and from the package's own type test intent.
findings.evidence: readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 define `rejectOnClear` as boolean; index.test-d.ts:28-29 expects invalid `rejectOnClear` values to be rejected at the type layer; index.js:12 only checks invalid truthy values.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused Node probe ran `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})`; observed `rejectOnClear 0 validation: accepted`. The same probe against `HEAD:index.js` observed `threw:TypeError`.

findings.title: Positive Infinity concurrency is rejected despite the existing implementation allowing it
findings.cause: The validation now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)` and removed the explicit `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance.
findings.impact: Consumers using `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)` as an unlimited mode can no longer construct a limiter, even though the previous implementation intentionally supported that value and the API accepts a numeric minimum of 1.
findings.evidence: index.js:127-130 rejects all non-integers; `git show HEAD:index.js` shows the prior guard allowed `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`; readme.md:37-44 documents the concurrency input as a number with minimum 1 rather than an integer-only finite number.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Focused Node probe ran `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)`; observed `Infinity concurrency: rejected:TypeError:Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up`. The same probe against `HEAD:index.js` observed `Infinity concurrency: accepted`.
